newsitem.title: USA: IBM announces Network Computer unit.
newsitem.headline: IBM announces Network Computer unit.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. said Monday it formed a new division to develop network computers, a new breed of scaled-down machines that cost far less to operate than personal computers.

The world's largest computer maker was the first in the industry to introduce one of the much-hyped devices -- also known as NCs -- which have no floppy disks, CD-ROM drives or huge operating systems taking up disk space.

In a memo to employees, IBM said it named Bob Dies, formerly general manager of the AS/400 minicomputer business, as general manager of the new Network Computer division. He will report to Robert Stephenson, senior vice president and group executive in charge of personal systems.
Network computers are scaled-down, diskless computers for accessing corporate networks and the Internet.

"Customer interest in our NC initiatives has been extremely high," IBM Chairman and CEO Louis Gerstner said in an internal company memo. "That's because customers are looking for solutions that lower the cost of desktop computing and provide access to networks."

The new division will coordinate all of IBM's efforts in network computers, including development of system architecture, hardware, software and network management. It will also lead IBM's efforts in defining industry standards for network computers and coordinate alliances with software developers and business partners who are creating software to links NCs with network servers.
Armonk, N.Y.-based IBM said it has no intention to abandon its personal computer business in favour of the emerging market for network computers, which some see as competing with PCs.

"Right now, many of our competitors are debating NC versus PC," Gerstner said in the memo. "For IBM, there is no debate. Many customers want and will continue to want full-function PCs. Many now want to explore the advantages of the NC. IBM will be a leader in both."

So far the current market is aimed at corporate users, who may begin to see NCs instead of a desktop computers hooked up to a network. NCs are not expected to replace PCs, but they are expected to take some share of the overall PC market.

Network computers do not have huge operating systems such as Windows or big applications that use space on a hard disk drive and take up memory space. They have small operating systems and temporarily use applications software and access data over corporate networks and the Internet.
Several companies have said in recent weeks that one PC can cost a corporation $6,000 to $12,000 a year to maintain, between software upgrades, diagnostics and other necessary maintenance.
IBM's stock rose 12.5 cents to $134.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
